### Problem: Next Permutation {#sec-part-p3-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `nums` of $n$ integers ($1 \le n \le 100$, $0 \le \text{nums}[i] \le 100$; values may repeat). Rearrange it **in place** to the *lexicographically next greater* permutation of its elements. If no greater permutation exists (i.e. `nums` is already the largest — non-increasing), rearrange it to the *smallest* possible permutation (non-decreasing / sorted ascending).

Lexicographic order between two permutations $a$ and $b$ is defined by the first index at which they differ: $a <_{\text{lex}} b$ iff at the smallest such $i$, $a[i] < b[i]$.

Source: [LC 31 · Next Permutation](https://leetcode.com/problems/next-permutation/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `[1,2,3]` → `[1,3,2]`. `[3,2,1]` → `[1,2,3]` (wrap around). `[1,1,5]` → `[1,5,1]`. `[1,3,5,4,2]` → `[1,4,2,3,5]`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Change the array as far to the right as possible. The longest non-increasing suffix is already the largest arrangement of its values, so the change must happen at the cell just before it, the pivot $i$: put there the smallest larger value from the suffix, then make the suffix as small as possible. The suffix is still non-increasing after that swap, so "sort it ascending" is just "reverse it", and the whole algorithm is $O(n)$.
:::

Think of the array as a number written in digits: the next permutation is "add one with the smallest possible change". The argument below is short, but every step of it is needed, which is why this problem is a favourite in interviews.

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Enumerate + lookup.** Generate all distinct permutations, sort them, find the input, take the next one (wrapping around). $O(n! \cdot n)$ time and space: only for $n \le 7$, and the oracle the other forms are tested against.
2. **Pivot + successor + sort suffix.** Find $i$, the rightmost index with `nums[i] < nums[i+1]`; find $j$, the rightmost index with `nums[j] > nums[i]`; swap them; sort `nums[i+1:]` ascending. If there is no $i$, reverse the whole array. $O(n\log n)$ because of the sort.
3. **Pivot + successor + reverse suffix.** The same, but the last step is a reversal, because the suffix is non-increasing after the swap (claim (c) below). $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra.

**Theorem (correctness of form 3).** Let $a$ be the input permutation of length $n$, and let $i$ be the pivot (or $-1$ if none).
- **(a) Nothing changes to the right of $i$ alone.** By the choice of $i$, $a[i+1] \ge a[i+2] \ge \cdots \ge a[n-1]$: the suffix is already its own largest arrangement, so any permutation larger than $a$ must differ from $a$ at index $i$ or earlier. The smallest such permutation keeps $a[0..i)$ and increases position $i$.
- **(b) The successor.** Since $a[i] < a[i+1]$, some suffix value exceeds $a[i]$. The suffix is non-increasing, so the values greater than $a[i]$ form a prefix of it, and the rightmost one, $a[j]$, is the smallest of them. Position $i$ must receive exactly this value: a smaller value is not an increase, a larger one gives a larger result.
- **(c) The swap keeps the suffix non-increasing.** After the swap, $a[i]_{\text{old}}$ sits at $j$. Its left neighbour $a[j-1]$ (if $j - 1 > i$) is $\ge a[j]_{\text{old}} > a[i]_{\text{old}}$. Its right neighbour $a[j+1]$ (if it exists) is $\le a[i]_{\text{old}}$, because $j$ was the *rightmost* value above $a[i]_{\text{old}}$. Every other adjacent pair of the suffix is unchanged.
- **(d) Reversal gives the least suffix.** A non-increasing sequence reversed is non-decreasing, the smallest arrangement of its values.
- **(e) Nothing lies in between.** The result agrees with $a$ on $a[0..i)$, has the smallest possible larger value at $i$, and the smallest arrangement of the rest after it. Any permutation strictly between $a$ and the result would have to agree on $a[0..i)$ and put at $i$ either $a[i]$ (then it is $\le a$ by (a)) or $a[j]$ (then it is $\ge$ the result by (d)). ∎

**No pivot.** If no $i$ exists, $a$ is non-increasing, the largest arrangement; the problem asks for the smallest, which is $a$ reversed.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Enumerate + lookup

::: {.form-next}
Do exactly what the definition says: list every distinct arrangement, sort the list, find the input and take the one after it, wrapping to the first. $O(n! \cdot n)$ time and space, so only for tiny $n$; it is the oracle for the stress tests.

**Worked example.** The $120$ arrangements of $[1,3,5,4,2]$ in order: the input is number $11$ (counting from $0$), and number $12$ is $[1,4,2,3,5]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("nperm", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 4, 2, 3, 5]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
from itertools import permutations

def next_perm_brute(nums):
    perms = sorted(set(permutations(nums)))
    k = perms.index(tuple(nums))
    return list(perms[(k + 1) % len(perms)])


assert sorted(set(permutations([1, 3, 5, 4, 2]))).index((1, 3, 5, 4, 2)) == 11
assert next_perm_brute([1, 3, 5, 4, 2]) == [1, 4, 2, 3, 5]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - std::next_permutation wraps for us
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
void nextPermBrute(vector<int>& a) {
    if (!next_permutation(a.begin(), a.end()))
        sort(a.begin(), a.end());
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The C++ tab uses `std::next_permutation`, which runs the same $O(n)$ algorithm as form 3 and returns `false` when it wraps around (leaving the range sorted ascending); the `if` restores that wrap explicitly for clarity. It is a convenient oracle in C++, as the full enumeration is in Python.

#### Pivot + successor + sort suffix

::: {.form-next}
Find $i$ (the rightmost ascent), find $j$ (the rightmost suffix value strictly greater than $a[i]$), swap, then sort `a[i+1:]`. $O(n\log n)$ because of the sort, and claims (a), (b), (e) prove it correct without needing (c). The next form changes only "sort" to "reverse".

**Worked example.** $[1, 3, 5, 4, 2]$: $i = 1$ ($a[1]=3 < a[2]=5$, and it is the rightmost ascent). $j = 3$ (rightmost with $a[j] > 3$ is $a[3]=4$). Swap: $[1, 4, 5, 3, 2]$. Sort $a[2:]$: $[2, 3, 5]$. Result: $[1, 4, 2, 3, 5]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("nperm", "sortsuf")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 4, 2, 3, 5]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def next_perm_sortsuffix(nums):
    a = list(nums)
    n = len(a)
    i = n - 2
    while i >= 0 and a[i] >= a[i + 1]:
        i -= 1
    if i < 0:
        a.reverse()
        return a
    j = n - 1
    while a[j] <= a[i]:
        j -= 1
    a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i + 1:] = sorted(a[i + 1:])
    return a
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
vector<int> nextPermSortSuffix(vector<int> a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    int i = n - 2;
    while (i >= 0 && a[i] >= a[i + 1]) --i;
    if (i < 0) { reverse(a.begin(), a.end()); return a; }
    int j = n - 1;
    while (a[j] <= a[i]) --j;
    swap(a[i], a[j]);
    sort(a.begin() + i + 1, a.end());
    return a;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> v{1, 3, 5, 4, 2};
    nextPermSortSuffix(v);
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The two `while` loops are the two searches: `a[i] >= a[i+1]` walks left *through* the non-increasing suffix (equal neighbours included), and `a[j] <= a[i]` walks left from the end *past* the values that are too small to be the successor. Both comparisons must be non-strict; the stress test below fails if either is made strict.

#### Pivot + successor + REVERSE suffix (optimal)

::: {.form-next}
Replace the sort by a reversal. That is valid only because the suffix is non-increasing after the swap, claim (c). The cost drops to $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory. This is the answer.

**Worked example.** Same $[1, 3, 5, 4, 2]$. After pivot/successor/swap: $[1, 4, 5, 3, 2]$. Reverse suffix $a[2:]$: $[5, 3, 2] \to [2, 3, 5]$. Result: $[1, 4, 2, 3, 5]$. Same as form 2.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("nperm", "optimal")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 4, 2, 3, 5]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0031-optimal
def next_permutation_inplace(a):
    """Mutates a to the lexicographic next permutation; returns False if wrapped."""
    n = len(a)
    i = n - 2
    while i >= 0 and a[i] >= a[i + 1]:
        i -= 1
    if i < 0:
        a.reverse()
        return False
    j = n - 1
    while a[j] <= a[i]:
        j -= 1
    a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    lo, hi = i + 1, n - 1
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo += 1; hi -= 1
    return True

# stress-test against the enumeration oracle (duplicates included) and the sort-suffix form
for _ in range(600):
    base = [random.randint(0, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 6))]
    a = list(base)
    next_permutation_inplace(a)
    assert a == next_perm_brute(base) == next_perm_sortsuffix(base)

board = [1, 3, 5, 4, 2]
next_permutation_inplace(board)
assert board == [1, 4, 2, 3, 5]   # the board sample

# wrap-around edge
tail = [3, 2, 1]
next_permutation_inplace(tail)
assert tail == [1, 2, 3]

# duplicates edge
dup = [1, 1, 5]
next_permutation_inplace(dup)
assert dup == [1, 5, 1]

# n=1 edge
one = [42]
assert next_permutation_inplace(one) == False
assert one == [42]
print("next_permutation_inplace OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
bool nextPermutationInplace(vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    int i = n - 2;
    while (i >= 0 && a[i] >= a[i + 1]) --i;
    if (i < 0) { reverse(a.begin(), a.end()); return false; }
    int j = n - 1;
    while (a[j] <= a[i]) --j;
    swap(a[i], a[j]);
    reverse(a.begin() + i + 1, a.end());
    return true;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> v{1, 3, 5, 4, 2};
    nextPermutationInplace(v);
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The one line to stare at is `while a[j] <= a[i]: j -= 1`, with $\le$. On $a = [1, 5, 1]$ the pivot is $i = 0$; scanning from the right, the trailing $1$ is skipped because $1 \le 1$, and $j$ lands on $5$, giving $[5, 1, 1]$. With a strict $<$ the scan would stop at the trailing $1$, swap two equal values, reverse the suffix and return $[1, 1, 5]$, which is smaller than the input.

::: {.callout-important title="Why reversing the suffix sorts it"}
After the swap only two neighbour pairs of the suffix change, $(j-1, j)$ and $(j, j+1)$. On the left, $a[j-1] \ge a[j]_{\text{old}} > a[i]_{\text{old}}$. On the right, $a[j+1] \le a[i]_{\text{old}}$, since $j$ was the rightmost value above $a[i]_{\text{old}}$. So the suffix is still non-increasing, and reversing a non-increasing sequence sorts it ascending in $O(n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Enumerate + lookup**: $O(n! \cdot n)$ time and space. **Pivot + successor + sort suffix**: $O(n\log n)$ time; $O(n)$ extra in Python (`sorted` builds a new list), $O(\log n)$ in C++. **Pivot + successor + REVERSE suffix (optimal)**: $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra; at most two backward scans and one reversal.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **$n = 1$**: no pivot; wrap case; reverse of a length-1 array is itself. Both `next_permutation` (C++) and our `next_permutation_inplace` return "wrapped" (false).
- **Already the largest** (non-increasing): wrap to sorted-ascending via the full-array reverse.
- **Strictly increasing**: the pivot is $i = n-2$ and the successor $j = n-1$; the last two elements are exchanged. (With equal values at the end, e.g. $[1, 2, 2]$, the pivot moves left: the answer is $[2, 1, 2]$.)
- **Duplicates**: handled because both scans use the *non-strict* comparison on the "walk through" side ($a[i] \ge a[i+1]$, $a[j] \le a[i]$).
- **All equal**: no pivot anywhere; reverse-the-whole-array is a no-op. Correct — there is no strictly greater permutation of a constant array.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CSES 1622 · Creating Strings](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1622) — print every distinct permutation of a string in order: start from the sorted string and call next permutation until it wraps.
- [LC 60 · Permutation Sequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/permutation-sequence/){difficulty="Hard"} — jump straight to the $k$-th permutation by unranking (@sec-part-rank) instead of stepping $k$ times.
:::
